path: Embedding propositional logic into first-order logic

results.title: Relation symbols of the propositional language
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: For a type of atoms, the family of relation symbols indexed by arity that consists of one nullary relation symbol for each atom $a$ and has no relation symbols of positive arity.

results.title: First-order language of propositional atoms
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a type of atoms, the first-order language whose relation symbols are exactly one nullary relation symbol for each atom, with no relation symbols of positive arity and no function symbols.

results.title: Embedding propositions as first-order sentences
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The translation of propositions over a type of atoms into sentences of the first-order language of propositional atoms, defined by recursion: an atom $a$ becomes the atomic sentence given by the nullary relation symbol of $a$, and $A \wedge B$, $A \vee B$ and $A \to B$ become the conjunction, the disjunction and the implication of the translations of $A$ and $B$.

results.title: Boolean structure of a valuation
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a valuation $v$ assigning a Boolean to each atom, the Boolean structure of $v$ is the structure for the first-order language of propositional atoms whose domain is the set of Booleans $\{\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{true}\}$ and in which the nullary relation symbol of an atom $a$ holds exactly when $v(a)$ is true. The language has no function symbols, so nothing else needs to be interpreted.

results.title: The embedding of propositions preserves truth-table semantics
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every valuation $v$ assigning a Boolean to each atom and every proposition $A$, the first-order sentence obtained by embedding $A$ is true in the Boolean structure of $v$ if and only if the truth-table value of $A$ under $v$ is true.

results.title: First central moment of the Bernstein weights
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `n ≠ 0`, `∑ k : Fin (n + 1), (x - k / n) * bernstein n k x = 0`: the binomial frequency `S / n` has mean `x`.

results.title: Fourth central moment of the Bernstein weights
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `n ≠ 0`, `∑ k : Fin (n + 1), (x - k / n) ^ 4 * bernstein n k x = x (1 - x) (1 + 3 (n - 2) x (1 - x)) / n³`, i.e. `E[(S - n x) ^ 4] = n x (1 - x) (1 + 3 (n - 2) x (1 - x))` for `S ~ Bin(n, x)`.

results.title: Fourth central moment bound for Bernstein weights
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The fourth central moment of the Bernstein weights is at most `1 / n ^ 2`, uniformly in `x ∈ [0, 1]`.

results.title: Voronovskaya's theorem (1932)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `f : ℝ → ℝ` of class `C²` and `x ∈ [0, 1]`, the Bernstein approximations of `f` on `[0, 1]` satisfy `n · (bernsteinApproximation n f x - f x) → x (1 - x) / 2 · f''(x)` as `n → ∞`.

outside: Wright–Fisher diffusion limit, generator form (Feller 1951; Voronovskaya 1932)

results.title: Sample mean over a set of units
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The mean of `y` over a set of units `S`, `(1/|S|) ∑_{i ∈ S} yᵢ` (the junk value `0` for `S = ∅`).

results.title: Sample variance over a set of units
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The sample variance of `y` over `S` with divisor `|S| - 1`; meaningful for `|S| ≥ 2` (for `|S| ≤ 1` it is the junk value `0`).

results.title: Mean of a finite population
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The mean of a finite population of `N = Fintype.card ι` units, `(1/N) ∑ᵢ yᵢ`.

results.title: Variance of a finite population
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The variance of a finite population with divisor `N - 1`, `S² = ∑ᵢ (yᵢ - ȳ)² / (N - 1)`; meaningful for `N ≥ 2`.

results.title: Finite-population average treatment effect
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The finite-population average treatment effect `(1/N) ∑ᵢ (y₁ᵢ - y₀ᵢ)`.

results.title: Difference-in-means estimator
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The difference in means for the treated set `S`: the mean of the treated outcomes `y₁` over `S` minus the mean of the control outcomes `y₀` over the complement.

results.title: Neyman's variance estimator
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Neyman's variance estimator `s₁² / n₁ + s₀² / n₀` for the treated set `S`.

results.title: Expectation of a statistic under complete randomization
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The expectation of a statistic `f` of the treated set under complete randomization: the treated set is uniform among the `(N choose n₁)` sets of `n₁` units (`n₁ ≤ N`; for `n₁ > N` there is no such set and the value is `0`).

results.title: Neyman (1923)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Under complete randomization with `n₁ ≥ 1` treated and `n₀ ≥ 1` control units, the difference in means is unbiased for the finite-population average treatment effect.

results.title: Neyman (1923)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The variance of the difference in means under complete randomization is `S₁²/n₁ + S₀²/n₀ - S_τ²/N`, where `S_τ²` is the population variance of the unit-level effects `τᵢ = y₁ᵢ - y₀ᵢ` and `n₀ = N - n₁`.

results.title: Expectation of Neyman's variance estimator under complete randomization
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The expectation of Neyman's variance estimator under complete randomization with at least two treated and two control units is `S₁²/n₁ + S₀²/n₀` (the sample variances are unbiased for the population variances under sampling without replacement).

results.title: Neyman's variance estimator is conservative
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Its expectation under complete randomization is at least the variance of the difference in means, with equality exactly when the treatment effect `y₁ᵢ - y₀ᵢ` is the same for all units.

results.title: Observed outcome from potential outcomes
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The observed outcome: `Y₁` on the treated event `T`, `Y₀` off it (consistency).

results.title: Propensity score
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The propensity of the event `T` given `W = w`, `P(T ∩ {W = w}) / P(W = w)`. Meaningful for `P(W = w) > 0`; it is `0` (a junk value) when `P(W = w) = 0`.

results.title: Conditional independence given a discrete variable
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The event `T` is conditionally independent of `V` given `W`, stated through the values of `W`: `P(T, V ∈ B, W = w) P(W = w) = P(T, W = w) P(V ∈ B, W = w)` for all measurable `B` and all `w`. For a `W` with countably many values this is the conditional independence of the indicator of `T` and `V` given `W`.

results.title: Strong ignorability
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Strong ignorability of the treatment `T` given `W` for the potential outcomes `V` (Rosenbaum & Rubin 1983): `T ⊥ V | W` and overlap, `0 < P(T | W = w) < 1` for every value `w` of positive probability.

results.title: Strong ignorability passes to functions of the potential outcomes
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Strong ignorability is inherited by measurable functions of the potential outcomes.

results.title: Rosenbaum & Rubin (1983), Theorem 1
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The propensity score `e(X) = P(T | X)` is a balancing score: given `e(X)`, the treatment is conditionally independent of the covariate `X`.

results.title: Calibration of the propensity score
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The propensity score is calibrated: among units with score `c` (an event of positive probability), the proportion treated is `c`.

results.title: Rosenbaum & Rubin (1983), Theorem 2
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A function `b(X)` of the covariate is a balancing score (`T ⊥ X | b(X)`) if and only if it is finer than the propensity score: covariate values of positive probability with the same `b` have the same propensity. (Theorem 1 is the case `b = e`.)

results.title: Rosenbaum & Rubin (1983), Theorem 3
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If treatment assignment is strongly ignorable given the covariate `X`, it is strongly ignorable given any balancing score `b(X)`.

results.title: Rosenbaum & Rubin (1983), Theorem 3
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Rosenbaum & Rubin (1983), Theorem 3 for the propensity score: if treatment assignment is strongly ignorable given the covariate `X`, it is strongly ignorable given `e(X)`.

results.title: Inverse probability weighting
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Inverse probability weighting (Horvitz & Thompson 1952; Rosenbaum 1987): under strong ignorability of `T` given a finitely-valued covariate `X` for the treated potential outcome `Y₁`, `E[1_T Y / e(X)] = E[Y₁]`, where `Y` is the observed outcome.

results.title: Inverse probability weighting
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Inverse probability weighting, control arm: under strong ignorability of `T` given `X` for `Y₀`, `E[1_{Tᶜ} Y / (1 - e(X))] = E[Y₀]`.

results.title: Identification of the average treatment effect by inverse probability weighting
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Under strong ignorability of `T` given a finitely-valued `X` for the pair `(Y₀, Y₁)`, `E[1_T Y / e(X) - 1_{Tᶜ} Y / (1 - e(X))] = E[Y₁ - Y₀]`.

results.title: Inverse probability weighting with a general covariate
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let the covariate information be a sub-σ-algebra `m` (for example the one generated by `X`), and `e = P(T | m)` the propensity score. If `Y₁` is integrable, the treatment is mean-ignorable for `Y₁`, `E[1_T Y₁ | m] = e E[Y₁ | m]` (implied by `Y₁ ⊥ T | m`), and overlap holds in the strong form `e ≥ ε > 0`, then `E[1_T Y / e] = E[Y₁]` for the observed outcome `Y`.

results.title: Sum of a nonempty list
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a nonempty list $(a_1, \dots, a_k)$ of elements of a type with an addition, its sum is obtained by adding the entries from left to right starting from the head: it is $a_1$ when $k = 1$, and $(\cdots((a_1 + a_2) + a_3) + \cdots) + a_k$ in general. No zero element is needed, and the proof that the list is nonempty does not affect the value.

results.title: The sum of a nonempty list does not depend on the nonemptiness proof
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $l$ of elements of a type with an addition and any two proofs $e_1$ and $e_2$ that $l$ is nonempty, the sum of $l$ computed with $e_1$ equals the sum of $l$ computed with $e_2$.

results.title: $B_h$-set
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be an additive commutative semigroup, $A \subseteq G$ and $h$ a natural number. $A$ is a $B_h$-set if $A$ is nonempty, $h \ge 1$, and whenever two sequences $(a_1, \dots, a_h)$ and $(b_1, \dots, b_h)$ of elements of $A$ satisfy $a_1 + \dots + a_h = b_1 + \dots + b_h$, the sequence $(b_1, \dots, b_h)$ is a rearrangement of $(a_1, \dots, a_h)$.

results.title: Edmonds' matroid intersection theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M_1$ and $M_2$ be matroids on a finite type $\alpha$, with arbitrary ground sets, and let $k$ be a natural number. There is a set $I \subseteq \alpha$ independent in both $M_1$ and $M_2$ with $|I| \ge k$ if and only if every $X \subseteq \alpha$ satisfies $k \le r_1(X) + r_2(\alpha \setminus X)$, where $r_i(Y)$ is the largest size of a subset of $Y$ independent in $M_i$.

results.title: Edmonds' matroid intersection theorem for matroids on the whole type
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M_1$ and $M_2$ be matroids on a finite type $\alpha$, each with ground set all of $\alpha$, and let $k$ be a natural number. There is a set $I \subseteq \alpha$ independent in both $M_1$ and $M_2$ with $|I| \ge k$ if and only if every $X \subseteq \alpha$ satisfies $k \le r_1(X) + r_2(\alpha \setminus X)$, where $r_i$ is the rank function of $M_i$.

results.title: Roman domination instances
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: An instance of ROMAN DOMINATION is a triple $(n, E, K)$ of a natural number $n$, the number of vertices, a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers, the edges, and a natural number $K$, the weight bound.

results.title: Graph of a Roman domination instance
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an instance $(n, E, K)$ of ROMAN DOMINATION, its graph is the graph of the edge list $E$ on $n$ vertices: the simple graph on $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ in which distinct vertices $i$ and $j$ are adjacent when $(i, j)$ or $(j, i)$ belongs to $E$.

results.title: Well-formed Roman domination instances
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An instance $(n, E, K)$ of ROMAN DOMINATION is well formed when the list $E$ has no repeated entries and every pair $(u, v)$ in $E$ has $u < n$, $v < n$, $u \ne v$ and $(v, u) \notin E$.

results.title: Feasible Roman domination instances
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An instance $(n, E, K)$ of ROMAN DOMINATION is feasible when there is a function $f$ from the vertices $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ of its graph to $\{0, 1, 2\}$ such that every vertex $v$ with $f(v) = 0$ is adjacent to some vertex $u$ with $f(u) = 2$, and the total weight $\sum_v f(v)$ is at most $K$.

results.title: ROMAN DOMINATION as a decision problem
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The decision problem ROMAN DOMINATION accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to an instance $(n, E, K)$ of ROMAN DOMINATION that is well formed and feasible; it rejects every other bitstring.

results.title: ROMAN DOMINATION is NP-complete
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The decision problem ROMAN DOMINATION belongs to NP, and every decision problem in NP reduces to it by a polynomial-time many-one reduction.

results.title: The machine that prepends a symbol
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a symbol $c$, this is the single-tape machine with two states that, from its start state, writes back the symbol under the head, moves left and enters its second state, and from its second state writes $c$ and halts without moving.

results.title: Prepending a symbol by stepping left
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $c$ be a symbol and $l$ a list of symbols, and consider the tape holding $l$ from the head rightwards, all other cells blank. Writing back the symbol under the head, moving the head one cell left, and then writing $c$ gives the tape holding the list $c$ followed by $l$ from the head rightwards, all other cells blank.

results.title: Prepending a symbol takes at most two steps
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every symbol $c$ and every word $l$, the machine that prepends $c$, started on $l$, halts with output the word $c$ followed by $l$ within at most two steps.

results.title: Correctness of the prepending machine
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every symbol $c$ and every word $l$, the machine that prepends $c$, started on $l$, halts with output the word $c$ followed by $l$.

results.title: Input code of a bit word
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a list of bits $w$, let $b_0, \dots, b_n$ be the reversal of $w$ followed by $\mathsf{true}$, reading $\mathsf{true}$ as $1$ and $\mathsf{false}$ as $0$. The input code of $w$ is the natural number $\sum_{i=0}^{n} b_i 2^i$. Its binary expansion, least significant bit first, is $b_0, \dots, b_n$: the input stack on which the single-tape emulation starts for the input word $w$.

results.title: Recovering a word from its input code
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list of bits $w$, reversing the binary encoding (least significant bit first) of the input code of $w$ and then dropping the first bit of the result gives back $w$.

results.title: Input decoding
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $m > 0$, let $b_0, \dots, b_n$ be its binary expansion, least significant bit first, without trailing zeros. The input decoding of $m$ is $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} b_{n-1-i} 2^i$, the value, least significant bit first, of the reversed expansion with its first bit dropped. The input decoding of $0$, whose expansion is empty, is $0$.

results.title: Computable predicates are decidable by single-tape machines
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a primitive recursive encoding into $\mathbb{N}$, and let $p$ be a computable predicate on $\alpha$, that is, one whose indicator function $\alpha \to \{0, 1\}$ is computable. Then $p$ is decidable by a single-tape Turing machine.

results.title: Pushing a cell onto a coded tape
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For any type $\Sigma$, an element $x$ of $\Sigma \cup \{\bot\}$ (with $\bot$ the blank) and a finite list $l$ over $\Sigma \cup \{\bot\}$, the push of $x$ onto $l$ is the empty list when $x = \bot$ and $l$ is empty, and otherwise the list obtained by prepending $x$ to $l$.

results.title: The head of a stack tape is the first entry of its list
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every one-sided tape $s$ over an alphabet $\Sigma$, stored as a finite list of cells in $\Sigma \cup \{\bot\}$ (with $\bot$ the blank) that does not end in $\bot$, the symbol at the head of $s$ is the first entry of that list, and the blank $\bot$ when the list is empty.

results.title: Tail of a stack tape, on cell lists
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $s$ be a stack tape, a one-sided tape stored as its list of cells without trailing blanks. Then the cell list of the tail of $s$ is the tail of the cell list of $s$, the tail of the empty list being empty.

results.title: Pushing onto a stack tape, on cell lists
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $s$ be a stack tape, a one-sided tape stored as its list of cells without trailing blanks, and $x$ a cell content, either a symbol or blank. Then the cell list of the tape obtained by pushing $x$ onto $s$ is the coded push of $x$ applied to the cell list of $s$: $x$ prepended to it, except that pushing a blank onto the empty tape gives the empty list.

results.title: Pushing a cell onto a coded tape is primitive recursive
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\Sigma$ be a type with a primitive recursive coding, and let $x$ be a cell content, either a symbol of $\Sigma$ or blank. Then the coded push of $x$, the map on lists of cell contents that prepends $x$ to a list, except that it sends the empty list to the empty list when $x$ is blank, is primitive recursive.

results.title: Binary codes of natural numbers in a tape alphabet are primitive recursive
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\Sigma$ be a type with a primitive recursive coding and $\iota$ any map from the Booleans to $\Sigma$. Then the map sending $n \in \mathbb{N}$ to the word over $\Sigma$ obtained by applying $\iota$ letterwise to the binary code of $n$ (least significant bit first, the empty word for $0$) is primitive recursive.

results.title: Halting is termination of the run
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A single-tape machine $M$ halts on an input word $l$ if and only if iterating the step function of $M$ from the initial configuration on $l$, until a configuration with no successor is reached, terminates.

results.title: Outputs are the ends of runs
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A single-tape machine $M$ outputs the word $l'$ on the input word $l$ if and only if iterating the step function of $M$ from the initial configuration on $l$, until a configuration with no successor is reached, terminates at the halting configuration for $l'$: the halting state, with $l'$ written from the head rightwards and every other cell blank.

results.title: Code of a single-tape configuration
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The code of a configuration of a single-tape machine is the quadruple consisting of its state (or the halting state), the symbol under the head (or blank), and the lists of cells, without trailing blanks, of the tapes to the left and to the right of the head.

results.title: The coded step commutes with coding
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every configuration $c$ of a single-tape machine $M$, the code of $c$ has no successor under the coded step exactly when $c$ has no successor under the step function of $M$, and otherwise the coded step sends the code of $c$ to the code of the successor of $c$.

results.title: The coded step of a single-tape machine is primitive recursive
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape Turing machine over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$, and fix primitive recursive codings of $\Sigma$ and of the states of $M$. Then the coded step of $M$, which maps a coded configuration to the coded configuration after one step of $M$ and has no value when the state is the halting state, is primitive recursive.

results.title: Running the coded step mirrors running the machine
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every configuration $c$ of a single-tape machine $M$, iterating the coded step from the code of $c$ until a coded configuration with no successor is reached terminates exactly when iterating the step function of $M$ from $c$ until a configuration with no successor is reached does, and then it ends at the code of the configuration where the run of $M$ from $c$ ends.

results.title: The code of the initial configuration is primitive recursive
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape Turing machine over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$, and fix primitive recursive codings of $\Sigma$ and of the states of $M$. Then the map sending an input word $w$ over $\Sigma$ to the code of the initial configuration of $M$ on $w$ is primitive recursive.

results.title: The final tape of a run is partial recursive in the input word
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape Turing machine whose finite alphabet $\Sigma$ carries a primitive recursive coding. The partial function sending an input word $l$ over $\Sigma$ to the final tape of the run of $M$ on $l$ (the symbol under the head, and the lists of cells to the left and to the right of the head), defined exactly when $M$ halts on $l$, is partial recursive.

results.title: The halting set of a single-tape machine is r.e
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape Turing machine over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$, and fix a primitive recursive coding of $\Sigma$. Then the set of input words over $\Sigma$ on which $M$ halts is recursively enumerable.

results.title: The halting set of a single-tape machine on binary inputs is r.e
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a single-tape Turing machine over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ and $\iota$ any map from the Booleans to $\Sigma$. Then the set of natural numbers $n$ such that $M$ halts on the word obtained by applying $\iota$ letterwise to the binary code of $n$ (least significant bit first, the empty word for $0$) is recursively enumerable.

results.title: A predicate recognized by a single-tape machine is r.e
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A predicate recognized by a single-tape machine is r.e.

results.title: A predicate decided by a single-tape machine is computable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The decider's answer is the symbol under the head of its final tape.

results.title: Single-tape decidable predicates are exactly the computable predicates
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is primitive recursive). A predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is decidable by a single-tape machine if and only if it is computable, that is, $p$ is decidable and its Boolean characteristic function $\alpha \to \mathrm{Bool}$ is computable.

results.title: Single-tape recognizable predicates are exactly the r.e. predicates
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is primitive recursive). A predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is recognizable by a single-tape machine if and only if it is recursively enumerable, that is, the partial function on $\alpha$ that is defined, with a trivial value, exactly where $p$ holds is partial recursive.

results.title: Single-tape co-recognizable predicates are those with an r.e. complement
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is primitive recursive). A predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is co-recognizable by a single-tape machine if and only if its complement $\neg p$ is recursively enumerable, that is, the partial function on $\alpha$ that is defined, with a trivial value, exactly where $\neg p$ holds is partial recursive.

results.title: Single-tape and multi-stack machines decide the same predicates
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Single-tape and multi-stack machines decide the same predicates.

results.title: Single-tape and multi-stack machines recognize the same predicates
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is primitive recursive). A predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is recognizable by a single-tape machine if and only if it is recognizable by a multi-stack machine.

results.title: Post's theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Post's theorem for single-tape machines: a predicate is decidable iff it is recognizable and co-recognizable.

results.title: Decidable predicates are recognizable by single-tape machines
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is primitive recursive). If a predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is decidable by a single-tape machine, then $p$ is recognizable by a single-tape machine.

results.title: Single-tape decidable predicates are co-recognizable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is primitive recursive). If a predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is decidable by a single-tape machine, then $p$ is co-recognizable by a single-tape machine, that is, its complement $\neg p$ is recognizable by a single-tape machine.

results.title: Single-tape decidable predicates are closed under complement
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is primitive recursive). If a predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is decidable by a single-tape machine, then so is its complement $\neg p$.

results.title: The halting problem for partial recursive codes is undecidable on single-tape machines
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, no single-tape machine decides whether a partial recursive code halts on input $n$.

results.title: The halting problem for partial recursive codes is recognizable on single-tape machines
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the set of partial recursive codes whose program halts on input $n$ is recognizable by a single-tape machine.

results.title: The halting problem for partial recursive codes is not co-recognizable on single-tape machines
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The halting problem for partial recursive codes is not co-recognizable on single-tape machines. For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the set of partial recursive codes whose program halts on input $n$ is not co-recognizable by a single-tape machine: no single-tape machine halts on exactly the codes whose program does not halt on input $n$.

results.title: Bloom filter
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A Bloom filter over a type $\alpha$ with $m$ bits consists of a finite list of hash functions $\alpha \to \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$ and a bit vector of length $m$.

results.title: Empty Bloom filter
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type and $m$ a natural number. Given a list of hash functions $\alpha \to \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$, the empty Bloom filter with these hash functions has all of its $m$ bits unset.

results.title: Bloom filter insertion
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Inserting an element $x$ into a Bloom filter keeps its hash functions and sets bit $h(x)$ for every hash function $h$ of the filter, leaving all other bits unchanged.

results.title: Bloom filter membership query
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A Bloom filter reports that an element $x$ may be present when bit $h(x)$ is set for every hash function $h$ of the filter, and reports $x$ absent otherwise.

results.title: Bits set by an insertion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $F$ be a Bloom filter over $\alpha$ with $m$ bits, let $x \in \alpha$ and let $i \in \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$. Bit $i$ of the filter obtained by inserting $x$ into $F$ is set if and only if bit $i$ of $F$ is set or some hash function $h$ of $F$ satisfies $h(x) = i$.

results.title: Membership query in terms of bits
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a Bloom filter $F$ and an element $x$, $F$ reports that $x$ may be present if and only if bit $h(x)$ of $F$ is set for every hash function $h$ of $F$.

results.title: An inserted element is reported present
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every Bloom filter $F$ and element $x$, the filter obtained by inserting $x$ into $F$ reports that $x$ may be present.

results.title: Insertion preserves positive answers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $F$ be a Bloom filter and let $x$, $y$ be elements. If $F$ reports that $x$ may be present, then so does the filter obtained by inserting $y$ into $F$.

results.title: The empty Bloom filter reports every element absent
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type, $m$ a natural number and $H$ a nonempty list of hash functions $\alpha \to \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$. For every element $x \in \alpha$, the empty Bloom filter with hash functions $H$ reports $x$ absent.

results.title: Lock mode
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: A lock is held in one of two modes: shared (a read lock) or exclusive (a write lock).

results.title: Lock mode coverage
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A lock mode $m'$ covers a lock mode $m$ when a lock in mode $m'$ permits what a lock in mode $m$ permits: an exclusive lock covers both modes, and a shared lock covers only the shared mode.

results.title: Lock mode required by an access
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The lock mode an access requires: shared for a read, exclusive for a write.

results.title: Action of a locked schedule
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: For $n$ transactions, numbered $0, \dots, n-1$, and a type $X$ of data items, an action of a locked schedule is one of three kinds: a read or write operation; a lock request, in which a transaction $t$ acquires a lock on an item $x \in X$ in a lock mode $m$ (shared or exclusive); or a release, in which a transaction $t$ releases its lock on an item $x \in X$.

results.title: Reads and writes of a locked schedule
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a locked schedule $s$, the schedule of reads and writes of $s$: its reads and writes in order, with the lock requests and releases erased.

results.title: Holding a lock
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $s$ be a locked schedule, $t$ a transaction, $x$ a data item, $m$ a lock mode and $p$ a natural number. Transaction $t$ holds a lock on $x$ covering mode $m$ just before position $p$ of $s$ when there is a position $q < p$ at which $s$ has a lock request by $t$ on $x$ in some mode $m'$ that covers $m$, and for no position $r$ with $q < r < p$ is the action of $s$ at $r$ a release of $x$ by $t$.

results.title: Schedules covered by locks
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A locked schedule $s$ is covered by locks when every read or write is protected by a lock of its transaction: whenever $s$ has at position $p$ a read or write $o$ by transaction $t$ on item $x$, just before position $p$ transaction $t$ holds a lock on $x$ (acquired at an earlier position and not released since) whose mode covers the mode $o$ requires, namely shared for a read and exclusive for a write; an exclusive…

results.title: Schedules that release every lock
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A locked schedule $s$ releases its locks when every lock request is followed by a matching release: whenever $s$ has at position $q$ a lock request (in either mode) by transaction $t$ on item $x$, there is a position $r > q$ at which $s$ has a release by $t$ of $x$.

results.title: Well-formed locked schedules
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A locked schedule $s$ (a list of reads, writes, lock requests and lock releases of transactions) is well formed when its accesses are covered by locks and it releases its locks: every read or write in $s$ is preceded by a lock request of its own transaction on its item, in a mode covering the access (shared or exclusive for a read, exclusive for a write), with no release of that item by that transaction in between;…

results.title: Lock compatibility at a point
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A locked schedule $s$ is legal just before position $p$ when, for every data item $x$, all distinct transactions $t \ne t'$ and all lock modes $m$, $m'$: if $t$ holds a lock on $x$ covering $m$ and $t'$ holds a lock on $x$ covering $m'$ just before position $p$ of $s$, then $m$ and $m'$ are both the shared mode. In words, two transactions do not both hold locks on the same item unless both locks are shared.

results.title: Locked items
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The list of data items locked in a locked schedule $s$: for each lock request of $s$, in order, the item it locks, so an item appears once for each lock request on it.

results.title: Legal locked schedule
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A locked schedule $s$ of length $\ell$ is legal when it satisfies lock compatibility at every point $p \le \ell$: just before position $p$, no two distinct transactions both hold locks on the same item unless both locks are shared.

results.title: Two-phase schedules
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A locked schedule $s$ is two-phase when every lock request of a transaction precedes every release of that transaction: whenever $s$ has at position $p$ a release by transaction $t$ and at position $q$ a lock request by $t$ (on any items, in any mode), then $q < p$.

results.title: Strict two-phase schedules
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A locked schedule $s$ is strict two-phase when it is two-phase and every transaction releases its exclusive locks only after its last read or write: whenever $s$ has at position $p$ a release by transaction $t$ of item $x$ and just before position $p$ transaction $t$ holds an exclusive lock on $x$, every read or write of $t$ in $s$ occurs at a position before $p$.

results.title: Lock coverage at a position
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a locked schedule $s$ and a position $p$: if $s$ has at position $p$ a read or write $o$ by transaction $t$ on item $x$, then just before position $p$ transaction $t$ holds a lock on $x$ whose mode covers the mode $o$ requires (shared for a read, exclusive for a write; an exclusive lock covers both modes). If position $p$ holds a lock request or a release, or lies beyond the end of $s$, the condition holds…

results.title: Release of the lock requested at a position
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a locked schedule $s$ and a position $q$: if $s$ has at position $q$ a lock request (in either mode) by transaction $t$ on item $x$, then there is a position $r$ with $q < r$ and $r$ less than the length of $s$ at which $s$ has a release by $t$ of $x$. If position $q$ holds a read, a write or a release, or lies beyond the end of $s$, the condition holds trivially.

results.title: Two-phase condition at a pair of positions
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a locked schedule $s$ and positions $p$ and $q$: if $s$ has at position $p$ a release by transaction $t$ and at position $q$ a lock request by the same transaction $t$, then $q < p$. For every other pair of positions, including positions beyond the end of $s$, the condition holds trivially.

results.title: Strictness at a pair of positions
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a locked schedule $s$ and positions $p$ and $q$: if $s$ has at position $p$ a release by transaction $t$ of item $x$, just before position $p$ transaction $t$ holds an exclusive lock on $x$, and $s$ has at position $q$ a read or write by $t$, then $q < p$. For every other pair of positions, including positions beyond the end of $s$, the condition holds trivially.

results.title: Release test
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a transaction $t$, this Boolean test on the actions of a locked schedule returns true exactly when the action is a release by $t$ of its lock on some item.

results.title: The two-phase locking theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If the reads and writes of a locked schedule are distinct, are covered by locks, and the schedule is legal and two-phase, then its reads and writes form a conflict-serializable schedule.

results.title: Strict two-phase locking theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If the reads and writes of a locked schedule are distinct, are covered by locks, and the schedule is legal and strict two-phase, then its reads and writes form a conflict-serializable schedule.

results.title: Binomial probability mass function
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The binomial probability `C(n, i) p^i (1 - p)^(n - i)` of `i` successes in `n` trials, as a function of `i : ℕ`. It vanishes for `i > n` (the binomial coefficient is zero there, so the truncated subtraction `n - i` is harmless).

results.title: Binomial upper tail probability
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The binomial upper tail `ℙ_p(X ≥ m) = ∑_{m ≤ i ≤ n} C(n, i) p^i (1 - p)^(n - i)`, Carter's `P(m)` with `p = ε / 3`.

results.title: Nonnegativity of binomial probabilities
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Binomial probabilities are nonnegative for `0 ≤ p ≤ 1`.

results.title: Positivity of binomial probabilities
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Binomial probabilities are positive on `{0, …, n}` for `0 < p < 1`.

results.title: Binomial probabilities vanish above n
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Binomial probabilities vanish above `n`.

results.title: Binomial probabilities sum to one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The binomial law sums to one (the binomial theorem), for every real `p`.

results.title: Nonnegativity of binomial tail probabilities
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Tail probabilities are nonnegative for `0 ≤ p ≤ 1`.

results.title: Binomial upper tail from zero is one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `P(0) = 1`, for every real `p`.

results.title: Binomial upper tail beyond n is zero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `P(m) = 0` for `m > n`.

results.title: Binomial upper tail as one minus a lower sum
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Carter's form of the tail: `P(m) = 1 - ∑_{i < m} Binom(i | n, p)`, for every `m`.

results.title: Recursion for the binomial upper tail
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: One step of the tail recursion: `P(m) = Binom(m | n, p) + P(m + 1)`.

results.title: Binomial upper tail is decreasing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `m ↦ P(m)` is antitone for `0 ≤ p ≤ 1`.

results.title: Binomial tails increase with the success probability
results.caption: Theorem

results.title: The binomial likelihood is unimodal in `p`, increasing part
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `a ≤ n` and `0 ≤ p ≤ p' ≤ a / n`, `Binom(a | n, p) ≤ Binom(a | n, p')`.

results.title: The binomial likelihood is unimodal in `p`, decreasing part
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `a ≤ n` and `a / n ≤ p ≤ p' ≤ 1`, `Binom(a | n, p') ≤ Binom(a | n, p)`.

results.title: Critical count of the mutation detection test
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Carter's critical count `k = min {m | P(m) ≤ FPR}` for the null success probability `p₀ = ε / 3` (Online Methods, before Eq. 9).

results.title: Randomization probability of the detection test
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The randomization probability `d = (FPR - P(k)) / (P(k - 1) - P(k))` of Eq. 9.

results.title: Power of the randomized mutation detection test
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The power `Pow(n, f) = P_f(X ≥ k) + d Binom(k - 1 | n, f)` of the exact-size randomized test (Carter et al. 2012, Eq. 9, with the randomization at `k - 1`; see the module doc).

results.title: Critical count meets the false-positive bound
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The critical count meets the false-positive bound: `P(k) ≤ FPR` (for `FPR ≥ 0`).

results.title: Upper bound on the critical count
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The critical count is at most `n + 1` (for `FPR ≥ 0`).

results.title: Positivity of the critical count
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The critical count is positive when `FPR < 1`.

results.title: Minimality of the critical count
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Minimality of the critical count: `FPR < P(k - 1)` (for `0 ≤ FPR < 1`).

results.title: Tail gap at the critical count
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The gap `P(k - 1) - P(k)` is the null probability of the boundary point `k - 1`.

results.title: The randomization is a probability
results.caption: Theorem

results.title: Exact size
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Exact size (Carter et al. 2012, Eq. 9 with the randomization at `k - 1`): under the null `f = p₀` the rejection probability is exactly `FPR`, for `0 ≤ FPR < 1`.

results.title: Detection power as a mixture of tail probabilities
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The power is the mixture `(1 - d) P_f(X ≥ k) + d P_f(X ≥ k - 1)` of two tail probabilities.

results.title: Power increases with the allelic fraction
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `Pow(n, f) ≤ Pow(n, f')` for `0 ≤ f ≤ f' ≤ 1`.

results.title: Power increases with purity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Power increases with purity at the ABSOLUTE allelic fraction `α s / (α q + 2 (1 - α))` of a clonal mutation of multiplicity `0 ≤ s ≤ q` (Carter et al. 2012, Eqs. 2, 9, 10).

results.title: Power decreases with local copy number
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Power decreases with local copy number at the ABSOLUTE allelic fraction, for a clonal mutation of multiplicity `0 ≤ s ≤ q ≤ q'` (Carter et al. 2012, Eqs. 2, 9, 10).

results.title: Power increases with multiplicity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Power increases with multiplicity at the ABSOLUTE allelic fraction, for `0 ≤ s ≤ s' ≤ q` (Carter et al. 2012, Eqs. 2, 9).
